newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov Pataki seen releasing welfare plan shortly.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov Pataki seen releasing welfare plan shortly.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki could release a detailed new welfare plan as soon as early next week but might not recall the legislature unless he sees a quick consensus, state and advocate sources speculated on Tuesday.

While the state Senate and the governor appear to have resolved at least some of their differences over the new program, that might not be the case for the Democrat-led Assembly, which blocked Pataki's previous welfare reforms.

The sources, some of whom declined to be named, said that the Republican governor likely will hold off on releasing his welfare plan and on deciding whether to hold a special session until the results of Tuesday's polls are fully evaluated.

If, for example, the Republican party's candidates did better than expected, the governor might feel more comfortable going ahead with a stricter plan than if the Democratic candidates were more successful than anticipated.

Pataki in mid-October said his goal was to call a special session after the elections to grapple with welfare. A spokesman for the governor noted he will talk with Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, and Assembly Leader Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, before making his decision.

"The governor, the last time he addressed the point, said that after the elections he would speak to Silver and Bruno, and see if we could move forward with some legislation on welfare, and if that was the case, it was the governor's goal to do that," said John Signor, a spokesman for the state Division of Budget.
He declined to comment about any of the details of Pataki's new welfare program and officials from the Assembly and Senate were not immediately available to comment.
The early signs about the shape of Pataki's new plan have raised alarms at some advocate groups, which fear they will be too harsh, though the Assembly might reject them.

"I'm hearing it's going to have a substantial reduction in benefits across the board, which is going to be anathema to the Assembly," said Rus Sykes, deputy director of the State Community Aid Association in Albany. The Assembly might fight cutting benefits at the same time as new federal workfare requirements are imposed, he explained.

The new federal welfare program, which was signed into law in August, gives some states, like New York, which have cut their welfare caseloads, bigger block grants because they are based on the year-ago number of people getting benefits.

But the rules allow states to cut how much they and their local communities contribute by as much as 25 percent without losing any federal funds, as they would have if they had chosen to make such reductions under the old welfare program.

As a result, New York City officials and welfare advocates fret that Pataki, who faces large, long-term budget gaps, will slash benefits to free up money to close these shortfalls. In its 1997 fiscal budget, New York State expects to spend about $1 billion on welfare, with its localities spending the same amount. Washington's share of the program is about $2 billion.

New York City accounts for 66 percent of the state's welfare caseload, and city officials fear that they will not get their fair share of the $2.4 billion federal grant the state expects to get under the new federal program.
State sources have said that while the Assembly is willing to work within the parameters set by the new federal plan, they might resist any efforts to further restrict the program.
For example, the Assembly again might block setting new 60- or 90-day time limits on the state-funded program, Home Relief, which ressemble ones the governor previously proposed.
And Sykes said that if Pataki, as now appears likely, proposes taking advantage of a new option under the federal law to curtail funds for mothers who have another child, the Assembly might object.
"I think that would be one the Assembly would never give in on," said Sykes, explaining the stiff workfare requirements alone probably are enough of a disincentive to have more children.

However, Pataki appears likely to propose one measure that could win substantial backing: a so-called earnings disregard, which would allow welfare recipients, and perhaps the working poor, to keep more of their paychecks.
